title: Authentication: sessions, tokens and passwords
problem: Passwords get stolen in bulk, sessions get hijacked, and a login that lives in one server's memory breaks the moment you add a second server.
summary: Authentication proves who is asking: salted adaptive hashes for passwords, an opaque session id in a hardened cookie or a signed bearer token for every request after login, a second factor that resists phishing, and single sign-on when an identity provider should own the login.
catTip: My collar tag says Cache, but the vet still checks the microchip. Proof once, then a wristband for the visit. If I lose the wristband, anyone wearing it is me until it expires, which is exactly why it expires.

recall.q: Your login works on one server but users get logged out at random once you add a second one. What is wrong, and what are the two standard fixes?
recall.a: Sessions are stored in each server's own memory, so a request that lands on the other server finds nothing. Either keep sessions in a shared store such as Redis referenced by an opaque session id in a cookie, or issue a signed bearer token that any server verifies locally; either way the servers themselves stay stateless.

guide.breaks: Fast unsalted hashes let a stolen table be cracked in hours, a cookie without flags is stolen by one script bug, and a login kept in one server's memory vanishes when the load balancer picks another server.
guide.tradeoffs: Every strengthening costs something: slow hashes burn CPU on each login, server-side sessions need a highly available store, self-contained tokens are hard to revoke, and extra factors add friction and account-recovery problems.
guide.explainSimply: Logging in is like checking in at a hotel: you prove who you are once and get a key card that opens your room until checkout. The card is just a random number the front desk can look up, so losing it is bad but the desk can cancel it instantly. A second factor is the desk also ringing your phone before handing it over.
guide.hint: Where does the session live right now, and where could it live so that any server can find it?

meow: Meow once at the desk, get a wristband. Meow at every door with the wristband. Lose the wristband, and whoever wears it meows as me.

quiz.prompt: A startup stores passwords as SHA-256 hashes with a per-user salt and asks whether to switch to Argon2id. What is the strongest reason to switch?
options: SHA-256 is broken and collisions can be found in seconds
SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so an attacker holding the table can test billions of guesses per second; Argon2id is deliberately slow and memory-hard
Argon2id does not need a salt, which simplifies the schema
Argon2id output is shorter, so the table takes less space
quiz.explanation: Password hashing must be expensive per guess; salting alone does not slow an attacker down. SHA-256 is not broken, Argon2id still uses a salt, and output length is irrelevant.

quiz.prompt: After a user logs in, the server keeps the same session id the browser already had before login. Which attack does this enable?
options: Session fixation: an attacker who planted that id in the victim's browser is now logged in as the victim
SQL injection through the session cookie
Replay of the TOTP code within its 30-second window
quiz.explanation: Fixation works because the pre-login id becomes the post-login id; regenerating the id on login breaks it. CSRF is about the browser attaching cookies to cross-site requests, not about which id is issued.

cards.q: List the three cookie flags a session cookie should carry and the attack each one blunts.
cards.a: Secure (no plaintext HTTP, so no network sniffing), HttpOnly (scripts cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it), SameSite=Lax or Strict (the browser does not attach it to cross-site requests, blunting CSRF). Add the host-only name prefix and Path=/ for good measure.

cards.q: A bank wants a second factor. Rank SMS codes, TOTP apps and passkeys by phishing resistance and say why.
cards.a: Passkeys (WebAuthn) are phishing-resistant because the browser signs only for the origin that registered the key. TOTP codes can be relayed by a fake page within the 30-second window. SMS is weakest: phishable plus SIM-swap and interception risk, which is why NIST SP 800-63B classes it as restricted.

glossary.note: Proof from two different factor types (know, have, are); WebAuthn passkeys are the phishing-resistant kind, SMS the restricted one.
One identity provider authenticates the user and sends your app a signed assertion (SAML) or ID token (OIDC); you never see the password.

sources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: Password Storage Cheat Sheet
sources.supports: Argon2id minimum of 19 MiB, 2 iterations, 1 parallelism; scrypt and bcrypt floors; the 72-byte bcrypt limit; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations; salting; the legacy-hash upgrade path

sources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.supports: 64 bits of session id entropy; Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain and Path guidance; the __Host- prefix; renewing the id after any privilege change; idle timeouts of 2-5 and 15-30 minutes

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management (July 2025)
sources.supports: 15-character minimum for single-factor passwords and 8 within MFA, no composition rules, no periodic change, blocklist check; PSTN/SMS out-of-band authentication remains restricted; at least one phishing-resistant option at AAL2

sources.title: RFC 6238, TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm (May 2011)
sources.supports: TOTP as HOTP with a time-based moving factor and the default 30-second time step

sources.title: W3C, Web Authentication: An API for accessing Public Key Credentials, Level 3
sources.supports: credentials scoped to the registering relying party's origins; passkey as the term for discoverable credentials
